links.reason: 1470 (பெருந்தேவி கைசோர்ந்து ... உயிர்பின்னும் வெற்றுடலம்) shows one queen faint or die; 293 (துணை முலையின் உள் அரங்கி மூழ்க ... புலம்பினாரே) shows a group of women wailing, and the verse itself never says the king is dead. There is no shared distinctive image, only the shared topic of mourners, and 'felt first by his women' is not in either Tamil text.
links.text_issue: 1470 sense uncertain (faint or death); 293 says nothing of the king in its own lines

links.reason: Both use நெய்சொரி/நெய்பெய் எரி, but it is a stock simile applied to two different things: a garland withered (988 கரிந்து பொன்னிற நைய) and a sulk flaring (1018 புலவி கூர்ந்ததே). The verses do not tie them to one man or say the second answers the first, so 'love and anger burning from the same man' is the grader's building, not the Tamil.

2060 hints that something lies above heaven (தன்பதன்கண் மிசையே) and 2068 has the sage set out how to reach இறுதியிலாப் பேரின்பம், so the two are in the same discourse and in order; but that is sequence in one teaching. Nothing in 2068 picks up the hint or answers it, and its own text is doubtful (உறுதிகணன்).

The prophecy (ஒருவன் மேல் கொற்றம் வைப்பின் நிலம் திரு நீங்கும்) and Kattiyankaran's pretext of a possessing deity (மாதெய்வம் ... செகுத்திடு நீ) are a real warning and the start of its fulfilment. But 241 shows the minister's own deceit, which points to his character, so the teaches claim that the epic locates the danger in the delegation before the man is not shown by this verse.

962 says that effort, vows and guarded senses (ஊக்கவேர் பூட்டி ... ஐம்பொறியின் வேலி காத்து) yield heaven then release; 1875 says only that the Lord has taken the soul as his field (உழவுகொண்டான்) and that praise and blame fall away. 1875 says nothing about release by grace, so the effort-against-grace contrast is supplied from outside, and only the farm figure is shared.

49 has the brother say the soul is other than the body (உடம்பின் வேறாம் உயிர்) and propose leaving it in the victors' refuge; 338 is the bird that leaves the nest (குடம்பை தனித்து ஒழிய). The epic does not use the bird image or call the tie light, so 'turning lightness into an act' is the note's gloss; the shared point is only that body and soul are separable.

2780 mocks the lamb sacrifice (மறியறுத்துக் கையா லுதிரந்தூய் ... தேவீர் உவந்து) and threatens repayment in நமனுலகு (நான்மடங்கு); 259 says not killing is better than a thousand oblations (அவிசொரிந்து ஆயிரம் வேட்டலின் ... உயிர்செகுத்து உண்ணாமை நன்று). Neither limits the other, so QUALIFIES does not fit, but the pair does show two grounds, punishment after death and comparative worth, for refusing the rite.

427 gives the ministers' reason for choosing Marusi (சுற்றமுங் கருமமுஞ் சொல்ல வல்லன்) and 578 has him promise a full report (இழிந்த சூழலும் ... புகன்ற மாற்றமும் சொல்லுகேன்). The second follows from the first in the plot; a promise to tell is not a test of his skill, so 'tested by his first act' overstates a sequence.

1483 is a funeral of a king of untainted fame (வஞ்சமில்லாப் புகழானை), not a proud one, and it never says rank failed to save him; 21 says even umbrella-bearing kings are carried off as dead (துஞ்சினார் என்று). The pair illustrates the common point that kings die. 1483 does not name the king, so the quatrain gains no named king.

Both name the three (அறிவு காட்சி ஒழுக்கம் in 240; ஓர்தல் தெளிவு ஒழுக்கம் with திரியோக மருந்து in 116), and the note is right that 116 frames them as medicine against birth while 240 lists heaven and rule as by-fruits (உம்பரின்பம் உலகிறைமை) beside release. That is a modest comparison of two framings; neither limits the other, so QUALIFIES is the wrong type.

1572 has the jester boast of defeating the Veda-learned in debate (வேதம் வல்லவரை வென்றிடு கிற்கும் வாதம்) and 1573 says how, by beating reciters (ஓதி வெல்லலுறு வார்களை) with a stick; they are adjacent verses of one speech, so this is sequence. 'Comic beating, not argument' depends on தடியாலே, which the marker itself marks as doubtful.

The note says Neelakesi 121 defines right faith as 'eight limbs' and a list of acts and freedoms; the Tamil says no such thing. 121 says faith is a clear longing (வேட்கையது தெளிவு) with the eight excellent things beginning with கடவுள் held in mind (எட்டுப்பொருள் மனத்துவைத்து), which is a list of objects of belief, not acts or limbs. The contrast the teaches builds on is therefore misdescribed.
links.text_issue: 241 sense uncertain; the third term may be faith or a part of it

links.reason: 78 lists சங்கு and திகிரி marks on the younger prince's hand; 109 has the court say Tivittan will guard the world under one umbrella (ஒருகுடை நீழற் காக்கும்) and that the prophecy is true. 109 never mentions the marks, and 78 does not name him, so reading the marks as signs of rule joins the two by story knowledge the verses do not state.

814 answers a doubt about plot (சிறுபடையவர் வென்று செகுப்பவோ) by the lion that kills many elephants; 500 says a jackal kills an elephant stuck in mud (காலாழ் களரில் நரி அடும்). These are not rival accounts of one thing: 500 is advice about ground, 814 an assertion that one strong fighter can rout many. Only the beast-over-elephant image is shared.

1577 lists the body's stuff (என்பு நரம்பு உதிரம் இறைச்சி தோல்) and nine doors, and 1578 (வினைப்பெருந் தச்சன்) makes the builder the deed; 894 lists diseases and calls the body நான்முகன் எடுத்த வீடு. The builder differs, but 894 is a lament and a litany to the Mother; its Brahma is idiom, not a doctrine put against karma, so the 'tension' and the two gains clauses are larger than the Tamil supports.

427 says Marusi can speak what is fit (உற்றன உய்த்துரைக்கும் ஆற்றலான்) and 529 has him confess he spoke unfit words (கறையவா மொழிகள் சொன்னேன்) and be ashamed, so the later scene does cut against the earlier claim. But 'at once' and 'recovery in 531' go beyond what the two verses show, and 529 is itself compressed and uncertain.

1240 only calls the god one who cut away the ghati karmas (காதிகண் அரிந்த); it does not say the worshipper's release comes from his own effort. 1527 does say grace as guru frees the soul (சத்தி குருவென வந்து ... தன்செயல் அற்றால்). A Jain-Saiva divide on this exists, but the epic verse does not state its side, so the claim that it 'carries a doctrine of self-won release' is an inference.

233 gives the freed soul its own குணம் (அனந்த அறிவு காட்சி வலி போகம்) and 444 gives the Lord the எண்குணம்; they share only the number eight. The two claims about who has eight qualities do not exclude each other, and 233 names only four, so 'tension' rests on a shared word.

1931 has hell's tormentors tell the sufferers to take the fruit of their earlier deed (முன்னதிற் செய்த வினையின்), and 198 has Death's servants bind those who said 'kill! stab!' and drive them with the same words. Both are punishers in hell, but the difference the note draws (servants of Death or of no one) is not a clash of claims; 1931 simply does not name a master.

27 is the prologue's one-line summary (அறம் கேட்டு ... அரசு அஞ்சித் துறந்த வாறும்) and 2811 is one verse of the later teaching (யாக்கை கொண்டவர்கட்கு யாவதும் துன்பம்). A preview and its scene is a fair link, but 27 names no content for the dharma, and 2811 is not 'the first body' of the sermon, since earlier verses of the chapter (such as 2780) already teach. The claim that the renunciation was a reply to this particular lesson goes beyond both texts.

Both verses have a king send the army to bring back the herd (தொறுமீட்க in 432, படுநிரை பெயர்க்க in 1858), a shared plot situation, not a distinctive image. Neither verse says the raid in 1858 was staged by friends or that the army of 432 was routed by hunters, so the contrast the teaches draws depends on plot outside both verses.

1494 says the lovers were like those who had won a state with neither death nor birth (சாதலும் பிறப்பும் இல்லாத் தன்மை), which does give love the language of release; 1103 asks whether Vishnu's world is sweeter than sleeping in a lover's arms (தாமரைக் கண்ணான் உலகு). The epic does not answer the couplet's question, and the 'two months' and the ending of that bliss are not in the verse, so the gains clauses outrun the Tamil.

Both poems have the friend comfort the heroine in the rains (இன்சொற் பலவும் உரைத்து in Kar Narpathu 9; வன்புறை இன்சொல் நன்பல பயிற்றும் in Akananuru 74), and Akananuru 74 does end by saying the herders' flute (குழல் வருத்தாக் காலே) would undo her. But these are two separate poems with different speakers and sceneries, so reading 74 as 'the heroine's answer' to 9 invents a dialogue; the pair shows a stock theme.

1453 has the fire weapon loosed (தீயொடு புணர்த்த) and 1454 has the Varuna arrow put it out in rain (வாருணம் ... தாரை நிரந்துவீழ்ந்தவித்தது). That is a counter, but it is two consecutive verses of one battle, which the plot record already gives. 'Matched counters' states the order of events and tells the reader nothing more.

1459 has the king's discus hide the hero in its fire (திகிரி கான்ற கனசுடர் வளைக்கப் பட்டு) and 1461 has the hero salute it and send it back to kill the king (மன்னனை மார்பு கீண்டு). That is a reversal and a real link, but not a tension, since nothing claims incompatible things, and the discus was the king's attack, not 'his whole safety'.

181 sets feeding jackals and dancing ghouls (நரிபறைந் துண்ணவும்) beside kings rising to heaven; Pattinathar's 354 has fire, worm, earth, kite, jackal and dog each claim the body. The carrion jackal is a stock figure, and the epic verse draws no moral about the body, so 'the field's feast is read as the fate of every body' is not in the Tamil and the teaches states only a shared theme.

365 says meditation burns the two deeds (தியானத்தின் இருவினை எரித்து); 219 says the fire, worshipped and risen, burns the deeds (அங்கி வினைசுடு). The epic's 'burn' is a figure for meditation, while 219 is a fire rite, so the clash is between a metaphor and a ritual, and the note's 'the Lord's fire' is not in 219. The Tirumanthiram line is obscure (வீழிசெய்து), and the 365 stanza has five lines.

Akananuru 168 has the waterfall roar like உதியன் அட்டில், the kitchen of one bound to giving; Purananuru 2 has பெருஞ்சோற்று மிகுபதம் வரையாது கொடுத்தோய் but no kitchen or noise, and the name உதியன் is not in its lines (only in the colophon). The link rests on the name and one reading of the feeding, and one simile cannot show that his food was 'proverbial'.

200 says the feet of the one beyond beginning are the refuge (அடிகளே சரணம்), and 138 says the holy feet are Sivam, Sivaloka, the path and refuge (திருவடியே தஞ்சம்). Both call the feet a refuge, but the contrast that the Jain refuge is only a means set apart from the goal rests on 202, which is not in the pair; 200 itself says nothing about a goal. 200 lines 1-2 are hard.

720 gives the lute-wood an earth-mother and a sky foster-mother (கைத்தாய்); 328 says only that Kandukkatan hands the child to the woman (நம்பியை நீட்டினான்), without the word or the image of a foster mother. Reading the lute's pedigree as a hint of Civakan's hidden birth is an authorial pattern supplied by the grader's account of the plot, not a shared image in the verses.

144 says that only the vows kept and the knowledge gained (விரதமும் ஞானமும்) go with the dead; 152 lists fast, worship of arhats and gifts, which win Indra's station, kingship and the end of the binding deed. The epic extends the idea of what a vow yields after death, so DEVELOPS fits better; but the first gains clause says the epic gains a ladder it already holds, and the epic adds worship and giving beyond the vow.

The two verses are about letters to the lord of Podanam, but 662 says only that after the reader reads (வாசகன் ... வாசினை செய்தபின்) the men repeat what it says (ஓலை கொடொப்ப உரைத்தர்), and nothing in it says the letter is a demand or who it is addressed to; that comes from 663 to 665. 514 is itself doubtful (the writer's name, line 4). A contrast of two letters is a plot link built on lines outside the pair.
links.text_issue: 662 line 3 clipped and line 4 short a syllable; 514 line 2 name and line 4 sense doubtful

links.reason: 22 has the king call for the unblemished twins (மக்களிரட்டையர் ... தந்தீக) and the man runs to find them; the verse says nothing of the goddess's anger, sacrifice or a plea to save the city. 327 (தன்னுயிர் நீப்பினும் செய்யற்க ... இன்னுயிர் நீக்கும் வினை) forbids killing even at the cost of one's life, so the Kural condemns the order; it does not need 'testing' against a ruler's duty, which neither text raises.

1101 pairs the priest's feeding of the fire (அங்கழல் அமைத்து மிக வேட்டான்) with the groom's longing (மனத்தின்மிக வேட்டான்), and Pattirakiriyar 147 asks when he will kindle the homa fire within to cross the sea of desire (ஓமக் கனல்வளர்த்தி உள்ளிருப்பது). The shared figure is the homa fire joined to desire. But in 1101 the fire does not serve desire, only sits beside it, so 'the same fire put to opposite uses' overstates it; SAME_IMAGE would fit.

947 has Civakan give the dying dog the five padas so that it leaves its body freed of the dark karma (நீனிற வினையின் நீங்கி); 1156 has a god feel his eye throb and think of the one dear as life (உயிரனானை நினைந்தான்) and rise through the sky. That the god is the dog and the one he goes to is Civakan is read from the story, since neither verse says it, but the good deed returning as help is the plain sense of the pair and the note states it correctly.
links.text_issue: 1156 does not name the god or the dog; sense uncertain

links.reason: 109 describes kings who stay in the courtesans' courtyards (ஆசைப் பட்டு அரசு வைக), part of a catalogue of the city's perfumes; 206 is the minister's warning that many sank in pleasure and met sin and blame (பாவமும் பழியும்). The first is a description of other kings and is not a charge against anyone; 'quietly prepares the charge' is the marker's gloss, not something 109 does.

Both use the plough-with-the-bow figure (வில்லுழுது வாழ்நர் in 17; வில்லேர் உழவர் in 872), which is a real shared image. But 17 never ranks the bowmen against anyone, and nothing in it makes the wound come from the man's word or promise (it says only நல்காது துறந்த, he left without grace), so the 'agrees' and the 'word' reading are the note's own.

620 names a king who strikes in anger without weighing and cannot bear a contrary word (மாற்றம் பொறான்); 389 praises the king who can bear bitter words (சொற்பொறுக்கும் பண்புடை வேந்தன்). The two do match, but the verse is a character sketch that shows what 389 praises by its opposite, and the pair adds only that proud kings are intolerant. The gains clauses say each lacks what the other has, which is true of any two separate texts.

2439 has the dresser print the tilaka with her nail and paint the eyes for the bride; 350 has the woman take off the tilaka with her finger, with earrings and pearls. The shared act of the tilaka and ornaments is real, but it is two adornment scenes in different chapters, with 350 the earlier, so 2439 does not 'open' what 350 'closes'; and nothing in either verse makes them incompatible claims.

395 has the world take refuge at the feet of the first lord (ஆழிக் காதியாம் பிரான்றன் சேவடி); 349 says the First gave the discus (ஆழி கொடுத்தனன்) to Achyuta. The only link is the word ஆழி, which may mean ocean or wheel in either verse, and 395 says nothing of bearing a wheel or of not passing it on. The 'rival firsts' claim is built on a doubtful word.

NM 66 has all the low delight in rice (நெல்லின் அரிசியான் இன்புறூஉம் கீழெல்லாம்) and the high in their due standing (வரிசையான் இன்புறூஉம் மேல்); ND 200 has the base fill on given rice (கயவர் ... சோறு ஆர்வர்) while effort-won water is nectar for others (தாளாண்மை நீரும் அமிழ்தாய் விடும்). The note is accurate and the contrast (labour against honour) is real, but neither extends the other, so DEVELOPS is the wrong type.

1472 has her உண்ணிறை and நாண் break (முடைந்தன) at the sight of the youth, and 1251 has the axe of desire break the door of நிறை bolted by நாண் (நாணுத்தாழ் வீழ்த்த கதவு). The word-pair and the verb are shared, and the Kural's image does explain why the two go together. But 1472 gives no sign that the poet treats it as an omen of the destined man, so that half of the teaches is not in the verse.

527 has the king say that only the deeds of a former birth strive (முன்னவன் செய்த ... வினைகளே முயல்வதல்லால்) and later effort cannot win what is not due; 377 says wealth is enjoyed only as the apportioner apportioned (வகுத்தான் வகுத்த வகை). Both put the lot beyond present effort, and the epic names the apportioner as past deeds. Nothing in 527 itself speaks of marriage or rank (the note takes that from the scene), and the verse is flagged as uncertain in lines 3-4.

990 has the girl say that if she forgot him (மறப்பனென்னின்) fate would drive her back to remember (விதி ... மீட்டு நினைப்பதே), and 1125 has the man say he would remember if he forgot, but he never forgets (மறப்பின் ... மறப்பறியேன்). The teaches is right that the epic puts the cause in fate. But the note's first gains clause is false: 990 already has the same logic that remembering follows forgetting, so the epic lacks nothing here.

claims.gist: the child of evil deeds, nursed by anger and fed on desire, wanders in the painful states of rebirth

claims_rejected.why: worship shown with its motive (desire for heaven's joy), not stated as a rule

claims.gist: a man shut in a pit and left to die showed no sign of a soul leaving, so there is no soul apart from the body

units.note: Taken as the materialist's test to be answered by the sage in the following verses; the stance could be read as reported.

claims_rejected.why: taunt that a lion fights a jackal, a point of counsel in the plot, not a doctrine
reports that the teacher gave faith, knowledge and conduct before ordaining; describes the act, states no doctrine
'like an illusion' is a lament's simile over the fallen king, not a stated doctrine of impermanence
reading marks of the body as signs of fortune is a prediction, not a school's claim
praise that a king without enemies protects himself and land, a description of one king

claims.gist: the Jina's teaching under the asoka tree is a nectar that ends the disease of birth
her daughter's love has settled on a learned man as the fruit of old deeds and stainless austerity

units.note: Karma ripening is voiced by a character in comfort, not endorsed by the narrator; I tagged it jain by the epic's frame.

claims_rejected.why: a taunt to warriors, rhetorical, not a stated norm
says the householder's dharma was taught but does not state it
narrates the king's rise by the lord's grace; an event, not a stated teaching

claims.gist: mercy shown to living beings with a pure mind brings everything one desires, as a cow gives milk
old karma goes with the soul like a bird and its shadow

claims_rejected.why: shows meditation and rebirth as a god in the story, but no one says that it is so
the Jina's destruction of karma is only the reason for a fragrance, too compressed to take as a claim
